articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designation Update
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This action updates OFAC's list of Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) and Blocked Persons.

Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated and the nature of the update were not immediately available in the initial announcement. Such updates are part of ongoing efforts to address threats posed by Iran.
The public is advised to consult the latest SDN list on the OFAC website for comprehensive information regarding this designation.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canadian Money Services Businesses for Facilitating Iranian Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight Canada-based money services businesses (MSBs) on November 6, 2026, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.' These entities are accused of operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy and facilitating sanctions evasion for the Iranian regime.

The designated MSBs, including Million Exchange, 1380079 BC Limited (Amin Exchange Vancouver), Top PC Technician Inc, NIA Nations (NIA Exchange), Farah Exchange, CCC Inc (C Exchange, Cryptoyal, Parsis Exchange), B Galaxy Inc (C Exchange, Cryptoyal), and Darvish Exchange, allegedly brokered transactions converting Iranian rials and other currencies into crypto assets.

Many of these businesses reportedly transacted with sanctioned Iranian crypto exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). This action was coordinated with the Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and FINTRAC, Canada's financial intelligence unit.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Under Cyber, Transnational Crime, and Cuba Sanctions Programs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting individuals and entities under its Cyber-related Sanctions, Transnational Criminal Organizations Sanctions, and Cuba Sanctions programs.

As part of this action, OFAC published a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically targeting the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy.'

The designations also included individuals and entities linked to global scam networks and the corporate infrastructure enabling them, such as individuals associated with the 'Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization' in Cambodia, and a Malaysian individual involved in cyber-related activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues Alert on Shadow Fleet, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings.

As part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' OFAC sanctioned 13 individuals and companies linked to a network providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's shadow fleet, which is used for illicit petroleum shipments. OFAC also targeted a Türkiye-based company supporting sanctioned Iranian airlines.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an alert warning against the use of falsely flagged vessels by Iran's shadow fleet and amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, authorizing certain transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of International Development Bank for Investment and Finance
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026.
This amended general license specifically authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

The issuance of such general licenses aims to provide clarity and a structured period for U.S. persons to conclude certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions regimes.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities Linked to North Korean IT Worker Fraud and DRC Destabilization
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in North Korean IT worker fraud and activities contributing to the destabilization of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Among the North Korea-related designations are individuals and an entity, First Financial and Technical Development Center, linked to DPRK IT worker fraud schemes targeting U.S. businesses. These individuals are accused of monitoring IT workers and ensuring they meet financial targets, often involving cryptocurrency transfers.

The DRC-related designations include the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, sanctioned for their alleged support of the M23 rebel group, which has contributed to the conflict and instability in eastern DRC.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company, JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, making it a blocked person.

OFAC determined that the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement emphasizes the importance of sanctions-related diligence during acquisitions, vigilance regarding sanctions risks, and adequate oversight of foreign operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026.

These amendments, affecting FAQs 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, are part of OFAC's ongoing review to ensure its published guidance remains current. The updated FAQs provide clarification on topics such as blocking and rejecting transactions, and filing reports with OFAC.

The revisions aim to provide clearer guidance for financial institutions and other U.S. persons on compliance procedures, including when to freeze funds, when to return them, and the timing and documentation requirements for reporting to OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Listings, and Amends General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

The action also included the issuance of Iran General License GG and HH, authorizing wind-down activities and limited safety and environmental transactions, respectively. Additionally, Russia-related General License 131K was issued, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026.

As part of this action, OFAC added several entities to its Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List (NS-MBS List), including Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Miracle Plus RMB Fund I), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Miracle Plus RMB Fund II), and Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Zhiyuan Enterprise Management Center Limited Partnership.

OFAC also issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based company, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and related services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company, making it a blocked person.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to the settlement amount.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

This deregulatory action aligns export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms, transferring them from the State Department's U.S. Munitions List to the Commerce Control List (CCL).

Under this new rule, BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of the newly controlled suppressors, including related software and technology, with license exceptions available for firearms also applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Closes Export Controls Loophole for Foreign-Owned Semiconductor Fabs in China
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has closed a loophole that previously allowed a handful of foreign companies to export semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology to China without a license.
This action by BIS now requires these foreign companies to obtain licenses for exporting their technology, placing them on par with their competitors.
The move aims to strengthen U.S. national security and foreign policy interests by ensuring that export controls work as intended and prevent the undermining of these objectives.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
